sections.html:
A Fort Myers owner works with two county offices. One decides what your property is worth: the Lee County Property Appraiser. The other mails the bill and receives your check: the Lee County Tax Collector.

Questions on value, exemptions or a changed mailing address go to leepa.org or 239-533-6100. For anything about paying, dial 239-533-6000. Your bill also names each authority that levies a tax, and those authorities answer for their own ad valorem rates and non-ad valorem assessments.

You can start paying November 1. The last day for the full amount is March 31 of the next year.

The best discount goes to November payers at 4 percent, then it steps down to 3 in December, 2 in January and 1 in February. Once April 1 arrives, any open balance is governed by the delinquent-tax statutes.

There are six ways to pay in Lee County.

  • Online through its pay site, with a printable receipt.
  • Kiosks at any of six service centers, by card or e-check; e-check payments are free.
  • Secure SmartLockers at the downtown Fort Myers, South Fort Myers, Cape Coral and Lehigh Acres centers, open around the clock. The Bonita Springs center takes drop-offs inside during business hours. Allow five business days.
  • By phone at 239-533-6000.
  • By mail, following the instructions on the bill.
  • In person at a service center.

The office posts payments within two business days after receiving them, and your account history online reads PAID or UNPAID.

Three arrangements let you pay over time or put off a bill, and the rules differ for each.

Lee County payment plans
PlanMain terms
Installment planApply November 1 to April 30; taxes over $100 per notice; four payments due June 30, September 30, December 31 and March 31, with discounts of 6, 4.5 and 3 percent on the first three
Partial payment planOpen to the current year; up to five payments an account; no discount; not taken online, and not for delinquent bills
Homestead deferralApply by March 31; age, income and lien limits; fire insurance naming the tax collector

For the 2027 tax year you can apply between November 1, 2026 and April 30, 2027. Should the home sell partway through, the buyer must keep the plan going for the rest of that year.

Miss the first installment deadline of July 31 and you are out of the plan. A normal notice goes out by November 1, and you will have to apply again next year.

  • If you skip the second or third payment, that amount is added to the next one.
  • A late installment of any kind costs you its discount.
  • Payment one equals a quarter of last year's gross tax; later payments can include half of any change to this year's taxes.
  • You stay enrolled from year to year so long as the first installment gets paid each time.

Any amount still owing on April 1 moves into the delinquent-tax process.

Your 2026 bill, due by March 31, 2027, is unaffected by Amendment 3. The amendment starts January 1, 2027, so whatever it changes will first appear on next year's bills. For its effect on your exemptions or assessment, ask the Lee County Property Appraiser.

In August you receive the TRIM notice (Form DR-474), a preview of proposed taxes. Public hearings on tentative budgets and millage follow in September and October, and final budgets and rates are heard in October and November.

The actual bill is mailed in November. Anyone contesting a value must file with the clerk inside 25 days of the notice. A surprise on the notice leaves you time to review your exemptions with the appraiser before the bill shows up.

Under Save Our Homes a homestead can gain no more than 3 percent or CPI in a year, whichever is less; the state chart shows 2.9 percent for 2025. Other property may rise 10 percent annually.

The appraiser's home page carries short videos about homestead and portability, the non-homestead limitation and estimating your taxes. Watch them before a sale or purchase, since the property resets to just value when it changes hands and the cap begins again.

Up to $50,000 of value comes off the taxable amount, in two pieces. The opening $25,000 lowers every levy, schools included. A second piece of up to $25,000 begins above $50,000 of assessed value and relieves only non-school levies.

  • The form is DR-501, and it goes to the appraiser by March 1.
  • The home must be your permanent residence on January 1.
  • Renting the unit, moving out for good or leaving Florida ends the exemption.
  • Older, disabled and military owners may have extra relief; ask the appraiser.

The bill for the whole year is addressed to the owner of record. Dividing it between buyer and seller is the closing agent's job.

The new deed is recorded with the Clerk of Court and then forwarded to the appraiser, and that lag explains why a seller can still receive a bill. An old mortgage company may also still be printed on the notice, so check that no escrow money is left. Your buyer files a separate homestead application by March 1.

To get ready, collect your deed, ID and latest tax bill, and pass the collector's payoff figure to the title agent. Read the draft settlement statement several days before the closing date. Cash buyers skip loan underwriting, so their closings can run on a shorter schedule.

April 1 makes a balance delinquent. The collector then auctions a certificate against the parcel by June 1, and the bidder willing to take the lowest interest rate wins, with bids falling in quarter-percent steps.

  • For two years after that April 1, the certificate holder has no claim on the owner.
  • Then a tax deed can be requested, for a $75 application fee.
  • The clerk conducts the auction, where the high bidder leaves a deposit of 5 percent or $200, whichever is larger.

A sale that closes before any of this starts keeps the payoff simple. If a certificate already exists, ask the collector for a redemption amount good through your closing date, and pass it to the title agent so it can be paid from your proceeds.

Furniture, appliances and other tangible personal property used when a home is rented can produce a separate tangible tax bill.

If you recently bought a home that is no longer rented, call the property appraiser's tangible office at 239-533-6140. Renting out a homestead can also end the exemption under state rules.

faqs.q: How do I pay Lee County tax on a Fort Myers home?
faqs.a: Pay the Lee County Tax Collector online, by phone at 239-533-6000, by mail, or at a service center. Six service centers have kiosks.
Call 239-533-6100, the appraiser's number. Exemptions, values and mailing addresses are handled there.

faqs.q: When does the installment plan application close?
faqs.a: It closes April 30 of the tax year, and applications for 2027 taxes opened November 1, 2026. The first payment is due by June 30.

faqs.q: Why did I get a bill after selling?
faqs.a: The roll lists the owner of record when bills go out, and a recent sale may not have reached the appraiser yet. Pass the bill to the buyer or closing agent.

faqs.q: Can I pay delinquent Fort Myers taxes by check?
faqs.a: Not by personal check or eCheck. Ask the collector which payment forms it accepts for delinquent real estate taxes.
